reason: Rows are unique 510(k) clearances, but the contract itself states they are not independent: one recall event names several 510(k) numbers and one firm recurs across rows (README.md:52; reproduction/construction.json:71). The two natural dependence units, recalling firm and recall event, are not available as keys: applicant is used inside the build but never shipped (reproduction/build.py:35,330; carry_columns is empty at construction.json:4), and the recall event identifier is label-side. product_code is the only shipped column that is a real source entity above the row. It is FDA's device-type code, and device_class and advisory_committee are exact functions of it in train (1,819 codes, zero exceptions). Hazards, recall causes and regulatory treatment are shared at device-type level, and 510(k) numbers co-listed on one recall are expected to be versions of one device family that normally stay in one product code. Training metadata supports using it: 0 missing values, 1,819 clusters in train, a one-way ANOVA intra-cluster correlation of the label of about 0.078 and an approximate design effect of 2.2, so row-level independence is visibly wrong at this level. The eval split has 1,128 product_code clusters with 0 missing, so the holdout should have enough clusters to resample. The key was chosen from source meaning and train-split descriptive statistics only, before holdout scoring; no eval or holdout metric was consulted.
limitations: Partial key. Firm-level dependence across different product codes (one firm's quality system, a firm-wide recall) is not captured, so intervals clustered on product_code can still be too narrow and should be read as a lower bound on uncertainty.

The assumption that 510(k) numbers co-listed on one recall event mostly share a product_code was not verified, because recall source rows were not read for this review. Events that span several product codes leave residual dependence between clusters.
Dependence between holdout rows and training rows (the same recall event or firm labelling rows in more than one split) is not addressed by any clustering inside the holdout.

Clusters are very unequal. In train the largest code holds 868 of 30,563 rows, the top 100 codes hold 53% of rows, 499 codes are singletons, and the effective number of clusters is about 209 (about 184 in eval). Cluster-resampled estimates will be dominated by a few large device types.

product_code is also a predictor, so its clusters mix heterogeneity in the signal with residual dependence. Resampling by product_code answers how performance varies over a new draw of device types, which is a different and wider question than variation over new clearances within the same device types.
product_code is a current-snapshot value. Whether FDA has re-coded old records was not checked, so cluster membership may differ from the code on the decision date.

Holdout product_code values were not inspected. No missing values occur in train or eval; if any holdout row has a missing product_code, treat that row as its own singleton cluster and do not pool the missing rows into one cluster.
The intra-cluster correlation and design effect were measured on train labels only and may differ in the holdout period.
